ety.text: From Middle English any, eny, ony, ani, aniȝ, eniȝ, æniȝ, from Old English ǣniġ (“any”), from Proto-West Germanic *ainīg, *ainag, from Proto-Germanic *ainagaz, from Proto-Germanic *ainaz (“one”), equivalent to one + -y. Cognate with Saterland Frisian eenich (“some”), West Frisian iennich (“only”), Dutch enig (“any, some”), Afrikaans enig (“any”), German Low German enig (“some”), German einig (“some”); via Proto-Indo-European *óynos cognate with Latin ūllus (“any”), Latin ūnicus (whence Italian unico (“unique”), French unique (“unique”)). Piecewise doublet of unique.

senses.d: To even the slightest extent; at all.
ex: 'That wouldn't surprise me any.'

senses.d: Used before different, before comparatives with more and less, and idiomatically before other comparatives, generally in interrogative, hypothetical, or negative contexts.
ex: If you get any taller, you'll start having to duck through doorways!
Is she any less enthused now that it's raining?

senses.d: Used to modify a verb, generally a finite verb or a non-finite verb in object position.
ex: That doesn't bother me any.
Unfortunately, I don't expect the documentation to help any.

senses.d: One at all; at least one; at least one kind of; some; a positive quantity of.
ex: Near-synonyms: some, all
Do you have any biscuits?

senses.d: A/an, each or some, no matter its/their identity or nature.
ex: Choose any item you want.
Any person may apply.

senses.d: An unspecified but imminent (second, minute, day etc.).
ex: They'll be arriving any day.
I expect the phone to ring at any moment.

senses.d: Any thing(s) or person(s).
ex: Any may apply.
I had put a bowl of fruit on the table, but the guests didn’t eat any (of it).

ety.text: Literally, “of the all”. Compare Italian del tutto, Spanish del todo, Portuguese de todo, Romanian de tot.

ety.text: Inherited from Late Latin nec ūnus (“not even one”). Compare Old French neisune, Italian nessuno and nissuno (Tuscan), Neapolitan nisciuno, Friulian nissun, Dalmatian nenčoin, Istriot ningun, Romanian niciun, Portuguese nenhum, Catalan ningú. By surface analysis, ni + uno.

senses.d: Any one out of an indefinite number of persons; anyone; any person.

senses.d: A person of some consideration or standing.

senses.d: In any way or manner whatever.
In any case. Used to indicate that a statement explains or supports a previous statement.
ex: Anyhow, he is dead now.

senses.d: Without care or tidiness; recklessly, negligently or randomly.
ex: It was a woman’s clothing, beyond a doubt, all thrown in anyhow, — as if the person who had placed it there had been in a desperate hurry.

senses.d: Any object, act, state, event, or fact whatsoever; a thing of any kind; something or other.
ex: I would not do it for anything.

senses.d: Expressing an indefinite comparison.

ex: He wasn't cooking, he wasn't sweeping, he wasn't anythinging!

senses.d: In any way, any extent or any degree.
ex: That isn't anything like a car.

senses.d: Used to indicate a change of subject.
ex: "I'll be ninety my next birthday, but Louella doesn't tell her age. Anyway, we're going to have you and Cynthia up for supper."

ety.text: From any + where.

senses.d: In or at any location.
ex: I don't know where I left my keys. They could be anywhere.
I'd rather be anywhere else.

senses.d: To (in the direction of) any location.
ex: Anywhere you go in France, there will be bread and wine with dinner.
I'm staying home today. I'm not going anywhere.

senses.d: Any location or an unknown location.
ex: Anywhere is better than here!

senses.d: A person without strong cultural or social ties that are exclusive to a specific place.

ety.text: From ove (“where”) + -unque (indefinite ending). Formed similarly to, and possibly influenced by, Latin ubīcumque.

From Middle English any time, ony tyme, from Old English ǣniġum tīman, equivalent to any + time.

senses.d: At any time.
ex: I don’t like beer much. Give me a fine wine anytime.

senses.d: suitable for any time; not associated with any particular time.
ex: they appeal to consumers looking for a cookie to eat with breakfast coffee or tea as well as an any-time snack.

ety.text: From Middle French tousjours, from Old French toz jorz, tuzjurz (“without ceasing”, literally “all days”). By surface analysis, tous + jours (compare Dutch altijd (“always”), Danish altid (“always”)). Replaced Old French sempres (“always”), from Latin semper. Cognate with Catalan and Occitan totjorn.
